title: Assad Sentenced to Death in Absentia, Houthis Kill Six in First Deadly Ship Attack, Lebanon Abolishes Capital Punishment
subhead: Syria's new government convicts its ousted dictator of war crimes, while Houthi strikes turn lethal in the Red Sea and Lebanon becomes the first Middle Eastern nation to end the death penalty — even as the region's wars grind on.

sections.heading: Syria Sentences Assad to Death in Absentia
sections.body:
A Syrian court has sentenced former President Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia after convicting him of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the country's civil war. The verdict, handed down on Tuesday in Damascus, drew celebrations from families of victims outside the courthouse, according to AP and BBC reports.

Assad, who was ousted in December 2024 and has reportedly been living in exile in Russia, was tried alongside several former officials including Atef Najib, the former head of the Political Security Branch in Daraa. The trial has been a centrepiece of Syria's post-revolution transitional justice effort.

The death sentence is largely symbolic — Assad is unlikely to face extradition from Russia — but it marks a formal break with the Assad era for the new Syrian government and provides a measure of legal accountability that victims' families have sought for over a decade.
sections.whyItMatters: The sentence formally closes one chapter of Syria's civil war and signals the new government's intent to pursue accountability, even if the practical effect on Assad himself is limited by his exile.

sections.heading: Houthis Kill Six in First Deadly Attack on Red Sea Shipping
sections.body:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement carried out its first lethal strike on a commercial vessel since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, killing at least six people and wounding ten more. According to BBC and AP reports, the group fired three ballistic missiles at the cargo ship Tihamah south of the port of Mocha, and then struck rescuers attempting to evacuate the wounded in a secondary attack.

Yemen's internationally recognised government said four crew members — three Pakistanis and one Indonesian — were killed, with a Yemeni coastguard reporting three further injuries during the rescue attempt. The Houthis claimed the vessel was carrying Saudi military equipment; the Yemeni government said it was carrying food.

This escalation marks a turning point in the Houthi naval campaign. Since launching attacks on shipping last month in parallel with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi strikes had damaged vessels but had not previously caused confirmed fatalities. The group's years-long truce with the internationally recognised Yemeni government also collapsed last month.
sections.whyItMatters: The attack introduces a deadly dimension to the Houthi maritime campaign just as global shipping is already rerouting around the closed Hormuz strait, compounding the disruption to world energy and trade flows.

sections.heading: US Fires Missiles at Blockade-Running Ship as Hormuz Talks Stall
sections.body:
US Central Command said an American helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged cargo vessel M/V Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman on Tuesday, disabling its steering gear after the crew 'ignored repeated warnings' from US forces. CENTCOM said the ship was attempting to transit to an Iranian port in violation of the US naval blockade.

According to CENTCOM's statement, the US has now redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to run the blockade, disabled three non-compliant vessels, and boarded two since the blockade was reimposed after the June memorandum of understanding collapsed. Al Jazeera reports that Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei declared the Strait of Hormuz 'will not be opened until the United States changes its behaviour and accepts Iran's conditions.' Meanwhile, Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi arrived in Tehran for talks with Iranian officials in the latest mediation effort.

President Trump also demanded on Monday that Iran pay compensation for '50 years' of damage — including for the 2000 USS Cole bombing — reversing the previous framing and further complicating negotiations. Al Jazeera's Tehran correspondent reported that the two sides 'are getting more and more distant when it comes to the possibility of any diplomatic settlement.'
sections.whyItMatters: The use of live missiles to disable a civilian vessel and the hardening of both sides' demands signal that the Hormuz standoff is escalating rather than moving toward resolution, with direct consequences for global oil markets.

sections.heading: Trump's Secret Plane Swap Reveals Depth of Iran Threat
sections.body:
President Trump confirmed on Tuesday that he secretly switched planes after leaving the NATO summit in Ankara last month due to what US officials described as a credible Iranian missile threat against Air Force One. According to the Washington Post, reported by BBC and AP, Trump was transported from Air Force One to a catering truck and then to a smaller C-32A military aircraft, while journalists and some White House staff remained on the decoy plane unaware that the president was no longer aboard.

Trump told reporters: 'I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, different plane.' Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the replacement aircraft separately using external stairs to make the flight appear routine. The clandestine operation came a day after the US renewed military strikes on Iran.

The incident underscores the personal stakes Trump faces in the conflict with Iran — a reality that sits uneasily with his public assertions that Iran's military has been 'thoroughly defeated.' BBC analysis notes that Iranian threats against Trump date to the 2020 killing of Qasem Soleimani and have intensified since the war began, with a '#KillTrump' banner displayed at Khamenei's funeral and a mural in central Tehran depicting Trump in a coffin.
sections.whyItMatters: The extraordinary security measure reveals that the Iranian regime's threats against the US president are considered credible enough to trigger a full decoy operation — a reminder that this war extends beyond the battlefield to direct threats against Western leaders.

sections.heading: Lebanon Becomes First Middle Eastern Country to Abolish the Death Penalty
sections.body:
Lebanon's parliament voted on Tuesday to abolish capital punishment, making it the first country in the Middle East and North Africa to do so. The legislation, which passed with a majority in the 128-seat chamber over Hezbollah's opposition, replaces the death penalty with life imprisonment with hard labour. It now goes to the cabinet and President Joseph Aoun for final approval, both of which are expected to sign.

Lebanon has not carried out an execution since 2004, though courts continued to impose death sentences. Rights groups estimate that over 78 people remain on death row. According to the BBC, campaigner Oragit Younan, who led a nearly three-decade effort to abolish capital punishment, said: 'We are in a war, and people have been killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win.'

The move stands in sharp contrast to regional trends: Jordan resumed executions in June, Israel has expanded the circumstances under which capital punishment can be imposed, and Iran has intensified its use of executions to suppress dissent, according to the UN human rights chief.
sections.whyItMatters: Lebanon's abolition of the death penalty — in the midst of regional war and domestic instability — is a striking rights achievement that sets a new benchmark in a region where capital punishment remains widespread and, in Iran's case, expanding.

sections.heading: Venezuela Restores Consular Ties With Israel as Latin America Realigns
sections.body:
Venezuela and Israel announced on Tuesday that they are restoring consular relations, 17 years after Caracas severed diplomatic ties over Israel's attacks on Gaza. The move follows a dramatic realignment since the US military abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January, with interim President Delcy Rodriguez pursuing closer ties with Washington and its allies.

According to Al Jazeera, Israel deployed a team to Venezuela after the country's twin earthquakes, and the consular agreement was framed as extending that emergency cooperation. Venezuela has also withdrawn from the International Criminal Court, aligning with the Trump administration's stance. Colombia's new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, recognised Israel's claim over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights on the same day.

The shift extends across Latin America: Chile and Honduras restored ambassadors to Israel last week, and Argentina's President Milei announced the relocation of its embassy to Jerusalem last year. Israel's regional ties, deeply strained during the Gaza war, are being rebuilt through a wave of right-wing electoral victories across the continent.
sections.whyItMatters: Venezuela's pivot from Iran-aligned to Israel-friendly is the latest domino in a broader Latin American realignment driven by right-wing governments and US influence, reshaping the diplomatic landscape of the Global South.

bottomLine: Assad's death sentence in absentia is a symbolic but real milestone for Syria's transitional justice, while the Houthi first lethal strike on shipping raises the stakes of the Red Sea dimension of the Iran conflict. The US military's use of Hellfire missiles on a civilian vessel and the stalling Hormuz talks show both sides hardening rather than converging. Trump's secret plane swap — smuggled out in a catering truck — reveals how personally the Iranian threat is felt at the top. Meanwhile, Lebanon's death penalty abolition and Venezuela's diplomatic pivot to Israel show that even amid war, the region's political landscape is shifting in significant ways.
